title: Use constant-time comparison when validating OTP codes
need_summary: Whether the OTP validation timing weakness is a security issue and how it was triaged, with the maintainer citing the Keycloak security policy page and classifying it as a weakness rather than a CVE.
security_topic: constant-time comparison for OTP validation
question_text:
Description

`HmacOTP.validateHOTP` and `TimeBasedOTP.validateTOTP` compare the generated one-time code against the user-supplied token with `String.equals`, which returns as soon as two characters differ. The submitted token is attacker-controlled input from the authentication form and the candidate is derived from the user's shared OTP secret, so this is a non-constant-time comparison of a secret-derived value (CWE-208).

The rest of the codebase already routes secret comparisons through `MessageDigest.isEqual`: client secrets (`OIDCClientSecretConfigWrapper`, `ClientAdapter`), recovery codes (`RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils`), the pre-authorized `tx_code` (`PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType`), MTLS thumbprints (`MtlsHoKTokenUtil`) and action codes (`CodeGenerateUtil`). The two OTP validators are the remaining outliers on the authentication path.

Proposal

Switch both OTP comparisons to `MessageDigest.isEqual`, keeping the existing null-safe behavior.

Affected code
- `server-spi/src/main/java/org/keycloak/models/utils/HmacOTP.java` (`validateHOTP`)
- `server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/models/utils/TimeBasedOTP.java` (`validateTOTP`)
answer_text:
Thank you for raising this. We usually ask you to submit security related issues  to the Keycloak security team as outlined in https://www.keycloak.org/security

For this one, I consider this that it is a weakness, and not a CVE, as the number of attempts to try this out wouldn't allow for a true timing attack.

I've triaged it as a weakness.

title: Keycloak V2 External-to-Internal Token Exchange Identity Provider Permission Bypass
need_summary: Whether the reported authorization bypass in Keycloak’s external-to-internal token exchange is real or mitigated by the experimental feature gate, anchored on the maintainer’s response and the linked removal issue/Keycloak security docs.
security_topic: applicability of an authorization-bypass report to an experimental token-exchange feature
question_text: A critical authorization bypass exists in Keycloak's V2 External-to-Internal Token Exchange implementation. The `ExternalToInternalTokenExchangeProvider` overrides the parent class method and **completely omits** the `AdminPermissions.management().idps().canExchangeTo()` authorization check. This allows **any confidential client** to exchange external identity provider tokens for internal Keycloak access tokens, bypassing all administrator-configured token exchange permission policies.
answer_text: Fortunately, this one in particular is hopefully not an issue as it needs experimental feature `TOKEN_EXCHANGE_EXTERNAL_INTERNAL_V2` . And that feature is going to be removed soon, probably in 26.7 - https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/48104 . The feature is replaced by JWT Authorization grant. See the details here: https://www.keycloak.org/securing-apps/jwt-authorization-grant and in the recent release notes. So please instead try to update your clients to use JWT Authorization grant instead of `TOKEN_EXCHANGE_EXTERNAL_INTERNAL_V2`

title: Brute-force detection: Authenticated session token refresh resets lockout counter
need_summary: Whether authenticated token refresh or SSO re-auth was incorrectly resetting brute-force lockout state, with the fix anchored in the maintainer comment describing the moved `logSuccess()` call.
security_topic: brute-force lockout counter reset via authenticated session refresh
question_text: When brute-force detection locks an account after repeated failed login attempts, a token refresh from an already-authenticated session on the same account resets the lockout state. This allows an attacker to resume password guessing before the lockout period expires, provided the legitimate user is actively using their account during the attack window. The attacker still must guess the correct password — this is a counter reset, not a bypass of password verification.
answer_text:
When an already logged in user triggerd a SSO re-auth, it was resetting the brute-force detection counter, and removing the temporary lockout.

Fixed it by moving the call to `logSuccess()` to the if-else statement just above it that checks if the login is coming from SSO. After this my failing test was passing.
thread_text:
ISSUE #49960: Brute-force detection: Authenticated session token refresh resets lockout counter
Author: abstractj
Date: 2026-06-12T13:23:10Z
Labels: area/authentication, kind/bug, priority/important, team/core-authn, backport/26.6, release/26.7.0
State: closed

[c0]
## Description

When brute-force detection locks an account after repeated failed login attempts, a token refresh from an already-authenticated session on the same account resets the lockout state. This allows an attacker to resume password guessing before the lockout period expires, provided the legitimate user is actively using their account during the attack window. The attacker still must guess the correct password — this is a counter reset, not a bypass of password verification.

## Version affected

26.5.7, 26.6.2

## Expected behavior

A successful cookie-based or token-refresh authentication from an existing session should not alter the brute-force lockout state. The lockout counter and timer should only be affected by explicit password-based authentication attempts. Existing sessions should remain active (locking them would enable attacker-triggered DoS), but they should be neutral with respect to lockout state.

## Actual behavior

When the locked account's legitimate user performs an action that triggers a token refresh (e.g., page reload in an already-authenticated browser), the "Temporarily locked" flag is cleared in the admin console and the lockout period is effectively cancelled. A subsequent login attempt from a different browser succeeds with the correct password despite the lockout window not having expired.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure brute-force detection on a realm (e.g., max login failures: 5, lockout duration: 15 minutes).
2. In Browser A, authenticate as the target user and remain logged in.
3. In Browser B, submit failed login attempts for the same account until the lockout threshold is reached.
4. In Browser B, confirm the account is locked by attempting to log in with the correct password — login is denied.
5. In Browser A, perform any action that triggers a token refresh (e.g., reload the page).
6. In Browser A, verify in the admin console that the "Temporarily locked" toggle is now disabled.
7. In Browser B, attempt to log in again with the correct password — login succeeds despite the lockout period not having expired.


---
*This issue was originally tracked in the private repository. Migrated by @abstractj.*

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @niels-van-nerum 2026-06-14T11:40:00Z:
Hi! I would like to resolve this as my first OSS-contribution. I am currently writing a test to verify the behavior, after that I will implement the fix. Could this be assigned to me?
---
[c2] @niels-van-nerum 2026-06-14T22:05:59Z:
I checked the `refresh_token` flow first, but couldn't produce a failing test for this issue, checked the code out some more, and saw a lead that make me think it was related to cookie-based SSO re-auth. So wrote a test for it and it failed!

When an already logged in user triggerd a SSO re-auth, it was resetting the brute-force detection counter, and removing the temporary lockout.

Fixed it by moving the call to `logSuccess()` to the if-else statement just above it that checks if the login is coming from SSO. After this my failing test was passing.
---

title: OIDC: Token introspection audience check validates azp instead of authenticating client when dynamic-scopes is enabled
need_summary: Whether the token introspection audience check regression caused by dynamic-scopes/parameterized-scopes was fixed, anchored by linked PR #48981 and the backport PR #50297 (with the maintainer noting it was previously fixed in issue #48980).
security_topic: token introspection audience-check regression with experimental scopes
question_text: The audience check should validate that the authenticating client (the one presenting credentials to the `/introspect` endpoint) is in the token's `aud`, regardless of whether `dynamic-scopes` is enabled.
answer_text: I have sent https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/50297 for 26.6. I'm closing this as it was fixed previously by https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/48980.
thread_text:
ISSUE #49794: OIDC: Token introspection audience check validates azp instead of authenticating client when dynamic-scopes is enabled
Author: abstractj
Date: 2026-06-08T18:26:52Z
Labels: area/oidc, kind/bug, action/missing-info, priority/normal, team/security, team/core-authn, team/core-protocols
State: closed

[c0]
## Description

The audience check added to the token introspection endpoint in PR #49131 (fixing CVE-2026-37979) does not work correctly when the `dynamic-scopes` experimental feature is enabled. In `AccessTokenIntrospectionProvider.introspectionChecks()`, the call to `transformAccessToken()` triggers dynamic-scopes scope resolution which calls `session.getContext().setClient(<azp client>)`, repointing the request context's client to the token's issued-for client. When `verifyAudience()` then reads `session.getContext().getClient()`, it gets the token's `azp` instead of the client that authenticated to the introspection endpoint.

This causes two problems: legitimate resource-server introspection returns `active:   false` (because the check becomes `azp in aud` instead of `authenticating-client in aud`), and confidential clients not in the token's audience can still read full claim sets from lightweight access tokens when `azp` happens to be in `aud`.

With dynamic-scopes disabled, the audience check works correctly.

## Version affected

26.6.2 (regression introduced by PR #49131, not present in 26.5)

## Expected behavior

The introspection audience check should validate that the authenticating client (the one presenting credentials to the `/introspect` endpoint) is in the token's `aud`, regardless of whether `dynamic-scopes` is enabled.

## Actual behavior

When `dynamic-scopes` is enabled, the check validates whether the token's `azp` is in `aud` instead. The event log confirms the wrong client is checked:

type="INTROSPECT_TOKEN_ERROR" error="invalid_token" reason="Client '<azp/frontend>' is not in the token audience"

The client named in `reason` is the token's `azp`, not the client that authenticated.

| token `aud` contains | introspecting client | `dynamic-scopes` | result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `account`, `api` | `api` | **on** | `active: false` |
| `account`, `api` | `api` | **off** | `active: true` |

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start Keycloak with `KC_FEATURES=dynamic-scopes`.
2. Create a realm with two clients: `frontend` (public) and `api` (confidential).
3. Obtain an access token via `frontend`. Ensure `api` is in the token's `aud` (e.g., via an audience mapper).
4. Call the introspection endpoint authenticating as `api` with the access token.
5. Observe `active: false` with the event reason naming `frontend` (the `azp`), not `api` (the authenticating client).
6. Disable `dynamic-scopes` and repeat — observe `active: true`.


---
*This issue was originally tracked in the private repository. Migrated by @abstractj.*

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @rmartinc 2026-06-09T08:59:19Z:
I cannot reproduce in current main. Nowadays there have been several changes in dynamic scopes (they have renamed to parameterized scope for example) and introspection worked as expected to me. I performed the commented reproducer steps:

1. Compile current  main and install it. You can use the nightly build instead (https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases/tag/nightly).
2. Start with parametrized scopes: `./kc.sh start-dev --features parameterized-scopes`.
3. Create a realm `demo` with the two clients, public `frontend` and confidential `api`. In the frontend one I have added a mapper to add an audience to `api`.
4. Perform the login using `frontend` and get an access token.
5. With that token I used the `api` client to call the introspection endpoint. Result is OK and the token is valid.

@abstractj This is not a weakness, this is a bug. I don't see any security issue here, the token simply doesn't work. [c5] @rmartinc 2026-06-23T14:44:20Z:

[c6] @u3r 2026-06-23T14:54:38Z:
@rmartinc it's been "experimental" for 4,5 years now, I think one can at least expect _basic_ functionality (like introspection) not to break in patch releases any more. Otherwise what is the point of trying things out?
Please, just cherry-pick the linked PR in the next patch release!

[c7] @abstractj 2026-06-23T20:05:49Z:
@u3r I understand this is frustrating, but let me clarify what "experimental" means in Keycloak, as defined in our [feature development process](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/blob/main/docs/features.md):

**Experimental features:**
- Are **not supported for production use-cases**, only for evaluation purposes
- Do **not have to be feature complete**
- Do **not have to provide backwards compatibility for APIs, nor migration support**

And specifically regarding breaking changes:

> *"Experimental features have no contract in terms of breaking changes. That means breaking changes can be introduced at any point, without new versions, deprecations, or any other warning. Additionally, no migration support is required."*

The duration a feature has been in experimental status does not change these guarantees — or the lack thereof. Features remain experimental until they meet the criteria for graduation to preview, which includes being feature complete, passing a security review, and resolving open feedback. The fact that parameterized scopes has been evolving (including the rename from dynamic scopes) is exactly why it is still experimental — it is under active development.

As @rmartinc confirmed, this appears to be already fixed on `main`. We encourage you to verify with the [nightly build](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases/tag/nightly). But backporting fixes for experimental features is not something we commit to — that is the trade-off of using them.

If you rely on this in production, that is at your own risk, and we strongly recommend waiting for the feature to graduate to at least preview status.
---
[c8] @u3r 2026-06-24T06:16:07Z:
@abstractj, @rmartinc  I have checked, and tested the linked PR #48981 with the 26.6.3 and it fixes the problem.
Would you please consider cherry-picking it in the course of your 26.6.4 release - IF such a release is anyway necessary?
That's all I dare ask at this moment.

However to facilitate people testing new features, I still think that breaking basic functionality in patch releases is bad.
I understand the nature of "experimental" but USUALLY that means: we break and adapt a feature to further it's development. Not because we fixed something else and it just broke completely.
---
[c9] @sschu 2026-06-24T06:34:59Z:
@abstractj @rmartinc Again, I want to stress my point that what broke is not the feature dynamic scopes, it is token introspection that broke. My expectation for an experimental feature is clearly that the feature might break or it might be changed and you cannot rely on the feature itself. You should still rely on the rest of Keycloak to work. If we don't guarantee this, nobody will ever activate an experimental feature on a production instance even for evaluation only and we will not get any feedback on it.

@stianst What's your take on this?
---
[c10] @rmartinc 2026-06-24T07:28:12Z:
@sschu What it's broken depends greatly in the feature. The parameterized scopes changes the way the scope is managed and how it is parsed. Using this feature can break a lot of things because it changes the internals about authorization parsing, don't expect us to fix things in experimental features. If you use experimental features, you can expect issues in everything to what the feature is related. I'm preparing a backport of #48981 and #48955, let's see what others think, but if a experimental feature touches a lot of things (like dynamic/parameterized scopes), they can affect everything. It's different to a feature that is limited to a single provider or similar.

[c11] @sschu 2026-06-24T07:48:59Z:
@rmartinc Thanks for the backports! I agree that due to the nature of the feature, it can interfere with other features and possibly break them. The question is if we are fine with this. Because as I said, this would make people way more reluctant to use any experimental feature on a production instance.

There is also a second problem in here: this regression wasn't detected by test automation as the token introspection tests are not executed both with and without dynamic scopes. This is independent of the feature state, it would also have happened if the feature was preview or default. In a perfect world, we would have to run all tests with all the possible ca. 2^70 combinations of features. Which is not going to happen but maybe we can identify which features affect what areas and run tests of that area with different combinations of those features? 
---
[c12] @rmartinc 2026-06-24T08:00:07Z:
Yes, this was not detected in the testsuite because it's a experimental feature, so it's not complete (for example in test coverage). As commented, experimental features is work in progress, in the last weeks we have been working in dynamic/parameterized scopes and that's why this issue was fixed in upstream. We cannot ensure anything about experimental features, because it's WIP, not completed. You cannot expect that a experimental feature is fully done, tested and everything since the first commit.

> Again, I want to stress my point that what broke is not the feature dynamic scopes, it is token introspection that broke. You should still rely on the rest of Keycloak to work. Yes, I agree. It's unfortunate that enabling some experimental feature may break some other parts, but as you mentioned, it's quite hard to verify it in the CI. You should never run the experimental feature in production, which is emphasized in docs/logs properly (I believe). IMO, the intention of using the experimental feature is to enable it in some dev/test environment, try only the specific functionality, and gather some feedback. So, it means that no harm should be done to your business or your real business data.

We'll try our best to keep the experimental features as "isolated" as possible, but for some features, it might be very challenging. Even with this issue and your insights, we got the necessary feedback, so we can react to it via these backports! 🚀  Thanks for that! :))

type="INTROSPECT_TOKEN_ERROR" error="invalid_token" reason="Client '<azp/frontend>' is not in the token audience"

The client named in `reason` is the token's `azp`, not the client that authenticated.

| token `aud` contains | introspecting client | `dynamic-scopes` | result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `account`, `api` | `api` | **on** | `active: false` |
| `account`, `api` | `api` | **off** | `active: true` |

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start Keycloak with `KC_FEATURES=dynamic-scopes`.
2. Create a realm with two clients: `frontend` (public) and `api` (confidential).
3. Obtain an access token via `frontend`. Ensure `api` is in the token's `aud` (e.g., via an audience mapper).
4. Call the introspection endpoint authenticating as `api` with the access token.
5. Observe `active: false` with the event reason naming `frontend` (the `azp`), not `api` (the authenticating client).
6. Disable `dynamic-scopes` and repeat — observe `active: true`.


---
*This issue was originally tracked in the private repository. Migrated by @abstractj.*

comments.author: abstractj
comments.body:
@u3r I understand this is frustrating, but let me clarify what "experimental" means in Keycloak, as defined in our [feature development process](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/blob/main/docs/features.md):

**Experimental features:**
- Are **not supported for production use-cases**, only for evaluation purposes
- Do **not have to be feature complete**
- Do **not have to provide backwards compatibility for APIs, nor migration support**

And specifically regarding breaking changes:

> *"Experimental features have no contract in terms of breaking changes. That means breaking changes can be introduced at any point, without new versions, deprecations, or any other warning. Additionally, no migration support is required."*

The duration a feature has been in experimental status does not change these guarantees — or the lack thereof. Features remain experimental until they meet the criteria for graduation to preview, which includes being feature complete, passing a security review, and resolving open feedback. The fact that parameterized scopes has been evolving (including the rename from dynamic scopes) is exactly why it is still experimental — it is under active development.

As @rmartinc confirmed, this appears to be already fixed on `main`. We encourage you to verify with the [nightly build](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases/tag/nightly). But backporting fixes for experimental features is not something we commit to — that is the trade-off of using them.

If you rely on this in production, that is at your own risk, and we strongly recommend waiting for the feature to graduate to at least preview status.

title: [CVE-2026-11986] FGAP v1 allows unassigning any role
need_summary: Whether CVE-2026-11986’s FGAP regression lets a user unassign roles they are not authorized to manage, with the answer anchored in commit 249d4e35b4a and the new RoleMappingDeleteResource endpoint.
security_topic: authorization regression in role unassignment
question_text: I'm not sure if it's a bug or intended...I have a user with view-users role. Then i have FGAP v1 through which I assign a role based policy to certain roles and also on users.map-roles. With keycloak 26.5.7 I could assign to a user only those roles and i could unassign only those roles. But now on versions 26.6.2 and 26.6.3 I can still assign only those roles, but I can unassign any other role from a user. Did something change in this direction? Is this intended?
answer_text:
The regression was introduced in commit 249d4e35b4a  fixing #46606.

This commit added a new Admin Console-specific endpoint `RoleMappingDeleteResource` at `rest/admin-ui-ext/src/main/java/org/keycloak/admin/ui/rest/RoleMappingDeleteResource.java` and switched the Admin Console from using the standard Admin REST API `DELETE /role-mappings/realm` to the new `POST /ui-ext/role-mapping-delete/users/{id}`.

But it is missing the per-role authorization check, it only performs user-level one.

title: Bearer token introspection uses the token client rather than the authenticated client for audience, if dynamic scopes is enabled
need_summary: Whether the bearer-token introspection audience bug is caused by the experimental dynamic-scopes feature and is a duplicate of issue #49794, which the maintainer links as the concrete source.

title: Organization managed users should not be allowed to link other idps from the account console
need_summary: Whether organization-managed users can bypass the intended identity-provider restriction by linking a different IdP from the account console, as reflected in the reported bug and the proposed flow-level deny workaround.

answer_text:
Current workaround I managed to have working till this gets merged in if anyone else is looking for it - 

You can hardcode an attribute for org related idp's using a mapper and add an explicit deny in your first broker login flow if the user has that attribute.

title: Keycloak Initialized status: "DOWN" hangs on 26.6
need_summary: Whether the startup hang on the Keycloak "Initialized" health check was a known issue fixed in 26.6.3, with the maintainer pointing to issue #48438 as the relevant anchor.
security_topic: startup hang / availability regression in async bootstrap mode
question_text: When starting up a fresh Keycloak instance on version 26.6.2 on Kubernetes, it gets stuck looping on this status indefinitely (I watched for 30 minutes before moving on):
answer_text: If this is only happening in async bootstrap mode, trying again with 26.6.3 would be good as https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/48438 was addressed - but it probably isn't related to the behavior you are seeing.
thread_text:
ISSUE #49693: Keycloak Initialized status: "DOWN" hangs on 26.6
Author: mateenkasim
Date: 2026-06-04T14:37:29Z
Labels: kind/bug, team/cloud-native, team/production-readiness, status/auto-expire, status/missing-information, area/observability
State: closed

[c0]
### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

observability

### Describe the bug

When starting up a fresh Keycloak instance on version 26.6.2 on Kubernetes, it gets stuck looping on this status indefinitely (I watched for 30 minutes before moving on):

```
INFO  [io.smallrye.health] (vert.x-eventloop-thread-0) SRHCK01001: Reporting health down status: {"status":"DOWN","checks":[{"name":"Graceful Shutdown","status":"UP"},{"name":"Keycloak database connections async health check","status":"UP"},{"name":"Keycloak Initialized","status":"DOWN"}]}
```

### Version

26.6.2

### Regression

- [x] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

Once deployed, Keycloak completes its initialization quickly, and the pods become ready in a timely manner. If there's an issue with startup, meaningful errors are logged.

### Actual behavior

The pods hang and loop on a down status with no indication of progress or errors.

The _only_ workaround seems to be to manually cycle the pod. After a restart, the pod comes up after about 40s, which matches earlier behavior. Once initialized, it doesn't do this again on later deploys/restarts, making this mainly a concern for fresh dev instances and new environments. It's critical to us that we can deploy without manual steps.

### How to Reproduce?

Details and what I've tried:
- Kubernetes, but not with the Operator. Deploying a StatefulSet and a couple services in line with the [Keycloak quick start repo](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak-quickstarts/blob/main/kubernetes/keycloak.yaml). Postgres DB.
- This first happened on 26.6.0 when that released and hasn't gone away since. This doesn't happen on 26.5.x.
- This happens in both a completely fresh minikube (MacOS Apple Silicon on Docker Desktop) with no data in it, and in cloud environments (x86) that migrate from 26.5.x.
- This happens whether the starting point is 0, 1, or 2 replicas.
- Using a pre-optimized built image for the following:
  - BouncyCastle FIPS bits
  - Custom themes for signup and account management
  - Added a custom protocol mapper
  - Enabling metrics, health, legacy token exchange, and FIPS
- Setting `KC_SERVER_ASYNC_BOOTSTRAP: "false"` removes the status messages, but it does not change the hanging behavior. Kubernetes cycled the pod after 10 minutes in this case.
- This doesn't seem to happen in a smaller Docker Compose setup.

### Anything else?

_No response_

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @shawkins 2026-06-04T17:47:19Z:
> Setting KC_SERVER_ASYNC_BOOTSTRAP: "false" removes the status messages, but it does not change the hanging behavior. Kubernetes cycled the pod after 10 minutes in this case.

To clarify does the hanging behavior happen in this case for both the fresh installs and for migrations?

> This happens in both a completely fresh minikube (MacOS Apple Silicon on Docker Desktop) with no data in it

With no data this behavior is not expected. If this is only happening in async bootstrap mode, trying again with 26.6.3 would be good as https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/48438 was addressed - but it probably isn't related to the behavior you are seeing.

If this is happening in either mode, then we need a thread dump to see what is causing the startup thread to hang.

> and in cloud environments (x86) that migrate from 26.5.x.

It is possible that a migration is in progress, please provide more information, such as logs.

title: Starting FIPS mode in 26.6.1 fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException
need_summary: Whether the FIPS startup failure was caused by a build-step ordering regression and hardcoded default truststore handling, with the answer anchored in the linked docs and PRs #44506, #45991, #45994, #46076, #48008, and PR #49359 as the reproducer/fix path.
security_topic: build-step ordering causing FIPS crypto provider initialization failure
question_text:
So the issue is:

When one sets FIPS to optional, that is:

* BCFIPS are bundled during container build
* KC_FEATURES=fips and relevant JDK flags (e.g. `-Dcom.redhat.fips=true`) are enabled based on the deployment parameters

ISSUE #49139: Starting FIPS mode in 26.6.1 fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException
Author: trixpan
Date: 2026-05-19T23:42:49Z
Labels: kind/bug, area/core, team/core-shared, release/26.7.0, team/core-protocols
State: closed

[c0]
### Before reporting an issue

- [x] I have read and understood the above terms for submitting issues, and I understand that my issue may be closed without action if I do not follow them.

### Area

core

### Describe the bug

The configureTruststore Quarkus build step lacks a dependency on CryptoProviderInitBuildItem, making its execution order relative to setCryptoProvider non-deterministic. In 26.5.7, the build step DAG coincidentally scheduled crypto provider initialization first. Changes in 26.6.1 (removal of UserProfileBuildItem steps, new createHttpAccessLogDirectory step, added @Consume(ProfileBuildItem.class) on health/resteasy steps) altered the DAG enough that configureTruststore now executes before the BouncyCastle FIPS provider is registered, causing KeyStore.getInstance("BCFKS") to fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException.

### Version

26.6.1

### Regression

- [x] The issue is a regression

### Expected behavior

FIPS compliant BCFKS works

### Actual behavior

KeyStore.getInstance("BCFKS") fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException

### How to Reproduce?

Start in FIPS mode with 

JAVA_OPTS="$JAVA_OPTS -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStoreType='BCFKS'"

### Anything else?

_No response_

[c7] @slaskawi 2026-05-27T10:07:20Z:
When reading this ticket, I see two separate issues:

1. DAG execution order change - the BouncyCastle Provider loading and setting up truststore executes shifted places leading to a failure. 
2. Hardcoded inclusion of the default Trust Store. 

## DAG execution order change

### Summary

It looks like Keycloak 26.5.7 scheduled `setCryptoProvider` earlier than `configureTruststore`. This changed in `26.6.1`, where `configureTruststore` runs earlier than `setCryptoProvider` leading to a failure

### Details

The `KeycloakProcessor.java` defines these methods in the following way:

``` java
@Consume(ProfileBuildItem.class)
@Produce(CryptoProviderInitBuildItem.class)
@BuildStep
@Record(ExecutionTime.STATIC_INIT)
void setCryptoProvider(KeycloakRecorder recorder) {...}

@Record(ExecutionTime.STATIC_INIT)
@BuildStep
@Consume(ConfigBuildItem.class)
void configureTruststore(KeycloakRecorder recorder) {...}
```

`configureKeycloakSessionFactory` properly consumes `CryptoProviderInitBuildItem`. `configureTruststore` does not. No happens-before edge in DAG → topo-sort order between them depends on what else changed.

`git diff 26.5.7..26.6.1 -- quarkus/deployment/.../KeycloakProcessor.java` indicated the following changes leading to this behavior:

1. **New `createHttpAccessLogDirectory` step**
2. **`UserProfileBuildItem` steps removed** — `parseDefaultUserProfileConfig` + `setDefaultUserProfileConfig` deleted
3. **`@Consume(ProfileBuildItem.class)` added on `disableHealthCheckBean` + `configureResteasy`**


### Related PRs

* [#45991](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/45991)
* [#45994](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/45994)
* [#46076](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/46076)
* [#48008](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/48008)

### Potential fix

The fix seems to be simple - add `@Consume(CryptoProviderInitBuildItem.class)` to `configureTruststore` build step in `KeycloakProcessor.java`

## Hardcoded default Trust Store issue

### Summary

After the new Kubernetes Trust Store detection has been merged ([#44506](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/44506)), Keycloak always adds the default Trust Store on the default execution path. This leads to the following failures:

  - **fips=optional (BCFIPS bundled, fips feature not enabled)**: `NoSuchMethodError: CryptoServicesRegistrar.checkConstraints` - non-FIPS BC instantiated against FIPS-flavored bcprov classes.
  - **fips=non-strict, JDK cacerts PKCS12**: `NPE: No password supplied for PKCS#12 KeyStore` while loading `/usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk/lib/security/cacerts`.

### Details

The [#44506](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/44506) indeed refactored adding the Kubernetes and OpenShift Trust Stores by default. However, the if none of these are present, the code returns exactly the same way as previously:

```java
//Pre-#44506 escape code path:
} else if (truststores.length == 0) {
    return; // nothing to configure — JDK default used directly
}

//The current version of it:
else if (truststores.size() == 0) {
    return; // nothing to configure, we'll just use the system default
}
```

The automatic inclusion of the Kubernetes and OpenShift Trust Stores can be activated with the `--truststore-kubernetes-enabled=false` option (@trixpan which I would recommend as a workaround here).

Analyzing the `fips=optional (BCFIPS bundled, fips feature not enabled)` case, I have an impression that we don't have any checks for this case - FIPS disabled but the BC libraries are present on the classpath. This probably requires a separate fix.

The `fips=non-strict, JDK cacerts PKCS12` seems to be another corner case when using the Default/System Trust Store, we should assume PKCS12 format. 

### Proposed fix

There are a few smaller things we could do here:

1. Introduce a check if BC is present in the `setCryptoProvider` and fail if it does and the FIPS mode is disabled. 
2. When loading the System Trust Store, we could first check the default password we use (`changeit`) and then the blank one. This might mitigate the NPE in password problem. 

But I honestly think the fixes here are more of a hardening compared to the `DAG execution order change` problem. 

## Final recommendation

At first, use the https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/49359 as a reproducer for the described problem. Ensure this fails correctly and fix the DAG dependency issue (potentially following the recommendation). Once this gets merged, consider opening follow up, focused issues for the `fips=optional (BCFIPS bundled, fips feature not enabled)` and `fips=non-strict, JDK cacerts PKCS12` cases.

comments.author: slaskawi
comments.body:
When reading this ticket, I see two separate issues:

1. DAG execution order change - the BouncyCastle Provider loading and setting up truststore executes shifted places leading to a failure. 
2. Hardcoded inclusion of the default Trust Store. 

## DAG execution order change

### Summary

It looks like Keycloak 26.5.7 scheduled `setCryptoProvider` earlier than `configureTruststore`. This changed in `26.6.1`, where `configureTruststore` runs earlier than `setCryptoProvider` leading to a failure

### Details

The `KeycloakProcessor.java` defines these methods in the following way:

``` java
@Consume(ProfileBuildItem.class)
@Produce(CryptoProviderInitBuildItem.class)
@BuildStep
@Record(ExecutionTime.STATIC_INIT)
void setCryptoProvider(KeycloakRecorder recorder) {...}

@Record(ExecutionTime.STATIC_INIT)
@BuildStep
@Consume(ConfigBuildItem.class)
void configureTruststore(KeycloakRecorder recorder) {...}
```

`configureKeycloakSessionFactory` properly consumes `CryptoProviderInitBuildItem`. `configureTruststore` does not. No happens-before edge in DAG → topo-sort order between them depends on what else changed.

`git diff 26.5.7..26.6.1 -- quarkus/deployment/.../KeycloakProcessor.java` indicated the following changes leading to this behavior:

1. **New `createHttpAccessLogDirectory` step**
2. **`UserProfileBuildItem` steps removed** — `parseDefaultUserProfileConfig` + `setDefaultUserProfileConfig` deleted
3. **`@Consume(ProfileBuildItem.class)` added on `disableHealthCheckBean` + `configureResteasy`**


### Related PRs

* [#45991](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/45991)
* [#45994](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/45994)
* [#46076](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/46076)
* [#48008](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/48008)

### Potential fix

The fix seems to be simple - add `@Consume(CryptoProviderInitBuildItem.class)` to `configureTruststore` build step in `KeycloakProcessor.java`

## Hardcoded default Trust Store issue

### Summary

After the new Kubernetes Trust Store detection has been merged ([#44506](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/44506)), Keycloak always adds the default Trust Store on the default execution path. This leads to the following failures:

  - **fips=optional (BCFIPS bundled, fips feature not enabled)**: `NoSuchMethodError: CryptoServicesRegistrar.checkConstraints` - non-FIPS BC instantiated against FIPS-flavored bcprov classes.
  - **fips=non-strict, JDK cacerts PKCS12**: `NPE: No password supplied for PKCS#12 KeyStore` while loading `/usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk/lib/security/cacerts`.

### Details

The [#44506](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/44506) indeed refactored adding the Kubernetes and OpenShift Trust Stores by default. However, the if none of these are present, the code returns exactly the same way as previously:

```java
//Pre-#44506 escape code path:
} else if (truststores.length == 0) {
    return; // nothing to configure — JDK default used directly
}

//The current version of it:
else if (truststores.size() == 0) {
    return; // nothing to configure, we'll just use the system default
}
```

The automatic inclusion of the Kubernetes and OpenShift Trust Stores can be activated with the `--truststore-kubernetes-enabled=false` option (@trixpan which I would recommend as a workaround here).

Analyzing the `fips=optional (BCFIPS bundled, fips feature not enabled)` case, I have an impression that we don't have any checks for this case - FIPS disabled but the BC libraries are present on the classpath. This probably requires a separate fix.

The `fips=non-strict, JDK cacerts PKCS12` seems to be another corner case when using the Default/System Trust Store, we should assume PKCS12 format. 

### Proposed fix

There are a few smaller things we could do here:

1. Introduce a check if BC is present in the `setCryptoProvider` and fail if it does and the FIPS mode is disabled. 
2. When loading the System Trust Store, we could first check the default password we use (`changeit`) and then the blank one. This might mitigate the NPE in password problem. 

But I honestly think the fixes here are more of a hardening compared to the `DAG execution order change` problem. 

## Final recommendation

At first, use the https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/49359 as a reproducer for the described problem. Ensure this fails correctly and fix the DAG dependency issue (potentially following the recommendation). Once this gets merged, consider opening follow up, focused issues for the `fips=optional (BCFIPS bundled, fips feature not enabled)` and `fips=non-strict, JDK cacerts PKCS12` cases.

title: Welcome page admin bootstrap bypasses local-only check when behind a same-host proxy without forwarding headers
need_summary: Whether the welcome-page admin bootstrap bypass via a same-host proxy is a real security issue and how it was addressed, anchored by the issue discussion and follow-up #49162.
security_topic: same-host proxy bypass of local-only admin bootstrap check
question_text: When Keycloak is deployed behind a reverse proxy or TCP forwarder running on the same host that connects to a loopback-bound Keycloak listener without injecting forwarding headers, the check is satisfied for remote requests. A remote user can access the bootstrap form and create the initial admin account.
answer_text: #49162 is now up-to-date with this, and I believe can close this issue.
thread_text:
ISSUE #49137: Welcome page admin bootstrap bypasses local-only check when behind a same-host proxy without forwarding headers
Author: abstractj
Date: 2026-05-19T19:26:27Z
Labels: area/admin/api, area/admin/ui, team/cloud-native, team/core-shared, priority/normal, team/security, release/26.7.0, kind/weakness
State: closed

[c0]
### Description

The initial admin creation form on the welcome page is guarded by `WelcomeResource.isLocal()`, which checks that both the remote and local addresses are loopback and that no `X-Forwarded-For` or `Forwarded` headers are present. When Keycloak is deployed behind a reverse proxy or TCP forwarder running on the same host that connects to a loopback-bound Keycloak listener without injecting forwarding headers, the check is satisfied for remote requests. A remote user can access the bootstrap form and create the initial admin account.

### Version affected

All current versions.

### Expected behavior

The welcome page admin creation form should not be accessible to remote users, regardless of whether a same-host proxy is in the request path. In production mode, dynamic admin creation via the welcome page should either be disabled entirely or require additional verification beyond network locality.

### Actual behavior

When a same-host reverse proxy or TCP forwarder connects to Keycloak over loopback without adding `Forwarded` or `X-Forwarded-For` headers, the `isLocal()` check passes for remote requests. The welcome page serves the admin creation form to any remote user accessing through the proxy.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a fresh Keycloak instance with no existing master admin user, bound to `127.0.0.1:8080`
2. Place a same-host reverse proxy or TCP forwarder in front of it, exposed on a remotely reachable interface, without configuring it to add `Forwarded` or `X-Forwarded-For` headers
3. From a remote machine, request the proxied `/` welcome page
4. Observe that Keycloak serves the "Create an administrative user" form instead of the "Local access required" warning
5. Submit the bootstrap form with a chosen username and password
6. The admin user is created successfully

### Anything else?

The impact is limited: the bootstrap form is only available on an uninitialized Keycloak instance with no sensitive data, and a legitimate admin would notice they are locked out. The team suggests considering disabling dynamic admin creation when starting Keycloak in production mode as a hardening measure. Related discussion: https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/discussions/48410


---
*This issue was originally tracked in the private repository. Migrated by @abstractj.*

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @shawkins 2026-05-19T23:20:08Z:
For the proxy to be involved, yet not set the headers this means that either:
- that the instance is setup for tls passthrough
- or the documentation has not be followed (https://www.keycloak.org/server/reverseproxy - you are told to set the proxy-headers option for non-https passthrough and to have the proxy always set the headers)

In tls passthrough if proxy-protocol is used, the client would still need to be local to pass the isLocal check.

So the security concern here is basically limited to tls passthrough when proxy-protocol is not enabled.

It's been discussed in issues related to #48410 whether we should require proxy-protocol to be used in passthrough, rather than introduce something like a proxy-mode setting.
---
[c2] @shawkins 2026-05-27T15:49:31Z:
@abstractj @vmuzikar @sschu @slaskawi based upon the review comments on the PR and our team discussion, I'm moving back to the issue to discuss the possible strategies here.

In prod mode the absolute safest approach, now that we have the bootstrap-admin command, is to disable by default the ability to create the initial admin via the welcome page. This means we won't have to make any assumptions based upon whether the proxy is setup correctly or the proxy settings are correct. If the option to allow creation via the web interface (e.g. --bootstrap-admin-web=true) was enabled, the check could still try to infer if the connection is local. The option though would document when this strategy may not work. This is however a potentially large breaking change.

The middle-ground, as shown on the PR, is to assume that the proxy and proxy settings are configured appropriately, which will limit when it's possible for the isLocal detection to not work as expected. However that could still be seen as breaking as without an additional option of some kind, a setup with tls passthrough and proxy-protocol not enabled won't be able create an admin via the welcome page. Note that if proxy-protocol were enabled, users can't currently use a standard browser to create the admin user as browser won't perform the proxy protocol - there is some overlap here with #48741

WDYT? Or should this be widened to all of keycloak-security?

And while it doesn't have to be done as part of this hardening, it seems like in dev mode the isLocal check could just return true.  This will improve usability when running in a container as the incoming connection is ofter not coming from localhost, but a different interface that keycloak has bound to within the container.
---
[c3] @sschu 2026-05-28T08:14:41Z:
@shawkins I am fine with the current approach. I also don't really see it as breaking because we don't really touch any existing installation but just change how you setup a new installation.
---
[c4] @slaskawi 2026-05-28T09:03:44Z:
Thanks for tagging me @shawkins !

> In prod mode the absolute safest approach, now that we have the bootstrap-admin command, is to disable by default the ability to create the initial admin via the welcome page.
> [...]
> If the option to allow creation via the web interface (e.g. --bootstrap-admin-web=true) was enabled, the check could still try to infer if the connection is local.
> [...]
> This is however a potentially large breaking change.

I like the general idea of introducing a switch, and making it possible to disable/enable the Welcome Page on demand. 

I also agree, this is a large breaking change. Some platforms, like [UDS Core](https://github.com/defenseunicorns/uds-core), heavily rely on it. But I also do appreciate there are other installations that do not care about it so much. 

In order to avoid introducing a breaking change, I would recommend using `--bootstrap-admin-web=false` with the default set to `true`. The "Configuring Keycloak for production" guide could clarify that disabling this option provides more hardened configuration.

> The middle-ground, as shown on the PR, is to assume that the proxy and proxy settings are configured appropriately, which will limit when it's possible for the isLocal detection to not work as expected. However that could still be seen as breaking as without an additional option of some kind, a setup with tls passthrough and proxy-protocol not enabled won't be able create an admin via the welcome page

Regardless to the path forward, I believe we should have a switch that will ignore additional checks. Otherwise it will be a breaking change for someone. 

Maybe we could consider something like: `--bootstrap-admin-web=[false|true|auto]`, where the `auto` mode would employ additional checks. Since we'll always have a switch to bring the previous behavior back - we won't leave users in a "hopeless place" without an option to get their previous behavior. 

> And while it doesn't have to be done as part of this hardening, it seems like in dev mode the isLocal check could just return true.

Sounds reasonable!
---
[c5] @shawkins 2026-05-28T14:35:49Z:
One more thing to point out - in the passthrough case the user would typically need to disable hostname validation to use a browser locally. 

We have two additional options based upon this:
- as mentioned in the PR, only do the new check if it's an https request. This allows users who have set --http-enabled=true to then create the initial admin over http
- allow sni to be enabled (which needs to be done in general), such that we can check the host used to access the server.

cc @vmuzikar

> Maybe we could consider something like: --bootstrap-admin-web=[false|true|auto], where the auto mode would employ additional checks. Since we'll always have a switch to bring the previous behavior back - we won't leave users in a "hopeless place" without an option to get their previous behavior.

@slaskawi To double check, are you suggesting that this would overlap with the relaxing of the dev mode:

--bootstrap-admin-web=[false|true|auto]

auto (default in prod): allow the first "local" user to create the bootstrap admin
true (default in dev): in dev mode this would be any access, in prod mode it would be the prior / relaxed notion of isLocal 
false: never allow the creation of the initial admin over the web interface

---
[c6] @vmuzikar 2026-05-29T07:46:52Z:
> In order to avoid introducing a breaking change, I would recommend using `--bootstrap-admin-web=false` with the default set to `true`.

-1, this would not solve the issue. If security is opt-in, and not secure by default, there's little reason to have that option at all, we might as well decide not to fix it.

I feel we're overthinking this here a bit with the `--bootstrap-admin-web` option. There's a security issue but the predicate here is misconfigured proxy (not using headers or PROXY protocol). Similar issue when proxy is misconfigured (and Keycloak can't reliably get the actual remote address) is affecting more areas like brute force detection. Maybe we should instead focus  on the root cause – can we detect in Keycloak that you are probably using a proxy but haven't configured Keycloak for it? I think we can, at least for locally running proxy (on the same host as Keycloak). We could reject requests with localhost as the remote address in non dev modes, when proxy headers or protocol are not configured. YEs, it is a breaking  change but it's a security fix which might be strong enough justification.
---
[c7] @slaskawi 2026-05-29T09:41:18Z:
> One more thing to point out - in the passthrough case the user would typically need to disable hostname validation to use a browser locally.

+1 - that seems like a good idea. 

@shawkins @vmuzikar I also wanted to suggest that we make it an explicit requirement that this feature works correctly with `kubectl port-forward` as this is the primary way Kube folks are expected to use it. 

> @slaskawi To double check, are you suggesting that this would overlap with the relaxing of the dev mode:
> If security is opt-in, and not secure by default, there's little reason to have that option at all, we might as well decide not to fix it.

@shawkins Yes, I think so, but at the same time @vmuzikar has a very good point here as well. 

> can we detect in Keycloak that you are probably using a proxy but haven't configured Keycloak for it

This sounds like a very interesting idea! However it might be a broader topic as we might want to at least have the "audit configuration" mode where Keycloak will allow these requests to pass through and "enforcing mode" where Keycloak would reject requests with an incorrect configuration. The Kubernetes [Pod Security Standards](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/) could be a good source of inspiration how to design these type of features. 
---
[c8] @shawkins 2026-05-29T12:19:26Z:
@vmuzikar sorry for introducing some additional confusion. We can absolutely focus on the hardening first, then circle back to whether a new option makes sense.

On the hardening, we can:
1. Keep building on the current PR with the HTTPS check. Thinking about it more, SNI doesn't help until we support multiple key certs - as you'd have to install one specifically for localhost.
 
2. The more I think about this, the more it seems related to https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/48741 / #47453. Along those lines we could think about adding the ability to create the initial user via the management port, which we never expect to be proxied, nor do we accept proxy settings for. Via the management port there would be no need for the isLocal check. If we go this route, we may also want to allow the management port to be independently enabled from health / metrics and eventually perhaps remove the ability of creating the initial admin user from main interface.
---
[c9] @vmuzikar 2026-05-29T12:30:52Z:
> create the initial user via the management port

If I understand @slaskawi's use case correctly, that would not work for them, correct? They would not want to expose the management port to their users?
---
[c10] @shawkins 2026-05-29T12:49:47Z:
> If I understand @slaskawi's use case correctly, that would not work for them, correct? They would not want to expose the management port to their users?

I don't think that is what @slaskawi is implying - there's no expectation that the main interface is being publicly exposed to create the initial admin. How ever they are doing it, it would still have to satisfy the isLocal check.
---
[c11] @shawkins 2026-05-30T13:38:08Z:
> Keep building on the current PR with the HTTPS check. Thinking about it more, SNI doesn't help until we support multiple key certs - as you'd have to install one specifically for localhost.

#49162 is now up-to-date with this, and I believe can close this issue.

The possible follow-ups are:
- relax isLocal for dev mode
- bootstrap-admin-web option, which could overlap with relaxing the isLocal check
- add the ability to create the initial admin on the management port, which would definitely be usable by port forwarding as well
---

In order to avoid introducing a breaking change, I would recommend using `--bootstrap-admin-web=false` with the default set to `true`. The "Configuring Keycloak for production" guide could clarify that disabling this option provides more hardened configuration.

> The middle-ground, as shown on the PR, is to assume that the proxy and proxy settings are configured appropriately, which will limit when it's possible for the isLocal detection to not work as expected. However that could still be seen as breaking as without an additional option of some kind, a setup with tls passthrough and proxy-protocol not enabled won't be able create an admin via the welcome page

Regardless to the path forward, I believe we should have a switch that will ignore additional checks. Otherwise it will be a breaking change for someone. 

Maybe we could consider something like: `--bootstrap-admin-web=[false|true|auto]`, where the `auto` mode would employ additional checks. Since we'll always have a switch to bring the previous behavior back - we won't leave users in a "hopeless place" without an option to get their previous behavior. 

> And while it doesn't have to be done as part of this hardening, it seems like in dev mode the isLocal check could just return true.

Sounds reasonable!

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
One more thing to point out - in the passthrough case the user would typically need to disable hostname validation to use a browser locally. 

We have two additional options based upon this:
- as mentioned in the PR, only do the new check if it's an https request. This allows users who have set --http-enabled=true to then create the initial admin over http
- allow sni to be enabled (which needs to be done in general), such that we can check the host used to access the server.

cc @vmuzikar

> Maybe we could consider something like: --bootstrap-admin-web=[false|true|auto], where the auto mode would employ additional checks. Since we'll always have a switch to bring the previous behavior back - we won't leave users in a "hopeless place" without an option to get their previous behavior.

@slaskawi To double check, are you suggesting that this would overlap with the relaxing of the dev mode:

--bootstrap-admin-web=[false|true|auto]

auto (default in prod): allow the first "local" user to create the bootstrap admin
true (default in dev): in dev mode this would be any access, in prod mode it would be the prior / relaxed notion of isLocal 
false: never allow the creation of the initial admin over the web interface

comments.author: vmuzikar
comments.body:
> In order to avoid introducing a breaking change, I would recommend using `--bootstrap-admin-web=false` with the default set to `true`.

-1, this would not solve the issue. If security is opt-in, and not secure by default, there's little reason to have that option at all, we might as well decide not to fix it.

I feel we're overthinking this here a bit with the `--bootstrap-admin-web` option. There's a security issue but the predicate here is misconfigured proxy (not using headers or PROXY protocol). Similar issue when proxy is misconfigured (and Keycloak can't reliably get the actual remote address) is affecting more areas like brute force detection. Maybe we should instead focus  on the root cause – can we detect in Keycloak that you are probably using a proxy but haven't configured Keycloak for it? I think we can, at least for locally running proxy (on the same host as Keycloak). We could reject requests with localhost as the remote address in non dev modes, when proxy headers or protocol are not configured. YEs, it is a breaking  change but it's a security fix which might be strong enough justification.

comments.author: slaskawi
comments.body:
> One more thing to point out - in the passthrough case the user would typically need to disable hostname validation to use a browser locally.

+1 - that seems like a good idea. 

@shawkins @vmuzikar I also wanted to suggest that we make it an explicit requirement that this feature works correctly with `kubectl port-forward` as this is the primary way Kube folks are expected to use it. 

> @slaskawi To double check, are you suggesting that this would overlap with the relaxing of the dev mode:
> If security is opt-in, and not secure by default, there's little reason to have that option at all, we might as well decide not to fix it.

@shawkins Yes, I think so, but at the same time @vmuzikar has a very good point here as well. 

> can we detect in Keycloak that you are probably using a proxy but haven't configured Keycloak for it

This sounds like a very interesting idea! However it might be a broader topic as we might want to at least have the "audit configuration" mode where Keycloak will allow these requests to pass through and "enforcing mode" where Keycloak would reject requests with an incorrect configuration. The Kubernetes [Pod Security Standards](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/) could be a good source of inspiration how to design these type of features.

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
@vmuzikar sorry for introducing some additional confusion. We can absolutely focus on the hardening first, then circle back to whether a new option makes sense.

On the hardening, we can:
1. Keep building on the current PR with the HTTPS check. Thinking about it more, SNI doesn't help until we support multiple key certs - as you'd have to install one specifically for localhost.
 
2. The more I think about this, the more it seems related to https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/48741 / #47453. Along those lines we could think about adding the ability to create the initial user via the management port, which we never expect to be proxied, nor do we accept proxy settings for. Via the management port there would be no need for the isLocal check. If we go this route, we may also want to allow the management port to be independently enabled from health / metrics and eventually perhaps remove the ability of creating the initial admin user from main interface.

comments.author: vmuzikar
comments.body:
> create the initial user via the management port

If I understand @slaskawi's use case correctly, that would not work for them, correct? They would not want to expose the management port to their users?

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
> If I understand @slaskawi's use case correctly, that would not work for them, correct? They would not want to expose the management port to their users?

I don't think that is what @slaskawi is implying - there's no expectation that the main interface is being publicly exposed to create the initial admin. How ever they are doing it, it would still have to satisfy the isLocal check.

comments.author: shawkins
comments.body:
> Keep building on the current PR with the HTTPS check. Thinking about it more, SNI doesn't help until we support multiple key certs - as you'd have to install one specifically for localhost.

#49162 is now up-to-date with this, and I believe can close this issue.

The possible follow-ups are:
- relax isLocal for dev mode
- bootstrap-admin-web option, which could overlap with relaxing the isLocal check
- add the ability to create the initial admin on the management port, which would definitely be usable by port forwarding as well

Author: martakat

### Description

### Summary
Keycloak 26.x (including the latest 26.6.1) depends on Quarkus 3.27.x, which pulls in Netty 4.1.125.Final and 4.1.130.Final.  
Both versions contain three critical Remote‑Code‑Execution vulnerabilities:

| CVE | CVSS | Brief description |
|-----|------|-------------------|
| CVE‑2026‑42581 | 9.8 | HTTP‑1.0 TE + CL smuggling bypass – arbitrary code execution. |
| CVE‑2026‑42584 | 9.1 | Race condition in `DefaultEventLoop` – remote code execution. |
| CVE‑2026‑42579 | 9.1 | `ChannelOutboundBuffer` overflow – remote code execution. |

Quarkus uses `quarkus‑netty` as its default HTTP server, so any client that can reach the service’s HTTP port can trigger these bugs.

### Upstream status
* Netty fixed the issues in **4.1.131.Final** (2026‑04‑02).  
* Quarkus upgraded to Netty 4.1.131.Final in **Quarkus 3.28.0** (2026‑04‑23).  
* Keycloak 26.x still ships with Quarkus 3.27.x, therefore the vulnerable Netty versions remain in the runtime artifact.

### Request

- Is there an estimated timeline or keycloak version which will include the updated quarkus version?

 _It would be great if the updated quarks version could be back-ported to Keycloak 26.5_

Thank you for your attention to this issue.

title: Investigate and plan what is needed for password hashing to be PQC ready
need_summary: Whether Keycloak’s password hashing algorithms are considered post-quantum safe, based on the investigation notes linked in the Google Sheets document and the maintainer’s summary that PBKDF2-SHA256 and Argon2id are PQC safe.
security_topic: PQC safety of password hashing algorithms
question_text:
Investigate supported password hashing algorithms in Keycloak and decide which if any are considered PQC safe.

As part of the investigation provide links to a document containing notes from the investigation, including findings and required actions.

If no PQC safe password hashing algorithms exist in Keycloak today the outcome of this investigation should be a refined sub-issue in https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/43690, including applicable sub-tasks.
answer_text:
- All current Keycloak password hashing algorithms (except deprecated SHA-1) provide adequate post-quantum security.  

- The default FIPS password hashing algorithm **PBKDF2-SHA256** and the default non-FIPS algorithm **Argon2id** are both PQC safe.  

- Other hashing algorithms e.g. SHA-256/384/512 etc are **not** used for password hashing (JWTs, Signatures, etc).

- Keycloak uses MD5 to generate caching keys for Idp/Client lookups, but this is only used for internal lookups and doesn't hold any important/sensitive data such as passwords. 

[Link to investigation document](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1jP9ZJGtJXrq-cijYq5vQ179zVieca_BceKbOJGhg8DY/edit?usp=sharing)

title: Investigate what is required for cookies to be PQC ready
need_summary: Whether Keycloak’s cookie signing and hashing scheme is sufficiently post-quantum safe, with the answer anchored in the maintainer’s cookie-type inventory and the linked follow-up issues #49858 and #49860.
security_topic: post-quantum readiness of cookie cryptography
question_text:
Cookies in Keycloak are currently signed by `HS512` by default. This should be PQC ready, but as part of this issue we should investigate to make sure all cookies are indeed PQC safe, or if some improvements are required.

As part of the investigation provide links to a document containing notes from the investigation, including findings and required actions.

If any issues are discovered as part of this investigate a refined sub-issue should be added to https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/43690 with applicable sub-tasks.
answer_text:
So keycloak is using HS512, AES128 and SHA256. The three of them are sufficient for post-quantum cryptography. In the case of AES128 and SHA256 it seems that there is a Grover's Algorithm that reduce the effective security in half, but as SHA256 only hashes the random generated session IDs (session and auth session ID) and AES is only used to encrypt the KC_RESTART we are safe. So better if we improve those two to use AES256 and SHA384/SHA512. Issues created for both:

* https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/49858
* https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/49860
thread_text:
ISSUE #48827: Investigate what is required for cookies to be PQC ready
Author: stianst
Date: 2026-05-08T08:50:05Z
Labels: priority/blocker, kind/task, team/core-authn
State: closed

[c0]
### Description

Cookies in Keycloak are currently signed by `HS512` by default. This should be PQC ready, but as part of this issue we should investigate to make sure all cookies are indeed PQC safe, or if some improvements are required.

As part of the investigation provide links to a document containing notes from the investigation, including findings and required actions.

If any issues are discovered as part of this investigate a refined sub-issue should be added to https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/43690 with applicable sub-tasks.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @rmartinc 2026-06-01T15:03:48Z:
The cookies that we are using in keycloak are the following (file `CookieType.java`):

| Java | Cookie | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
|AUTH_DETACHED | KC_STATE_CHECKER | internal encoded token signed with HS512 |
|AUTH_RESTART | KC_RESTART | internal encoded token signed with HS512 and encrypted using AES128 |
|AUTH_SESSION_ID_HASH | KC_AUTH_SESSION_HASH | SHA256 hash of the authentication session ID |
|AUTH_SESSION_ID | AUTH_SESSION_ID | Base64 of the auth session ID and signature using HS512 signer context (id.signature) |
|IDENTITY | KEYCLOAK_IDENTITY | internal encoded token signed with HS512 |
|LOCALE | KEYCLOAK_LOCALE | locale plain string ("en" or "es") |
|LOGIN_HINT | KEYCLOAK_REMEMBER_ME  | Just plain "username: " + urlencoder of the username |
|SESSION | KEYCLOAK_SESSION | Base64Url of the SHA-256 of the ID of the session |
|WELCOME_CSRF | WELCOME_STATE_CHECKER | Just base64url of 256 random bits (32 bytes) |

So keycloak is using HS512, AES128 and SHA256. The three of them are sufficient for post-quantum cryptography. In the case of AES128 and SHA256 it seems that there is a Grover's Algorithm that reduce the effective security in half, but as SHA256 only hashes the random generated session IDs (session and auth session ID) and AES is only used to encrypt the KC_RESTART we are safe. So better if we improve those two to use AES256 and SHA384/SHA512. Issues created for both:

* https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/49858
* https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/49860

title: Investigate and plan what is needed for SAML 2.0 to be PQC ready
need_summary: Whether Keycloak’s SAML 2.0 flow needs PQC/hybrid signature support to avoid downgrade attacks, anchored by the RFC9231bis draft and the linked W3C strategy issue plus the implementation milestone #50292.
security_topic: PQC readiness for SAML 2.0 signatures and encryption
question_text: Many of the algorithms used by SAML 2.0 endpoints and assertions are not considered PQC-safe. We need to investigate what new algorithms we need to support, including reviewing if some hybrid signing algorithms are required. This should cover all usage of cryptography in Keycloak in SAML 2.0 endpoints and assertions, including server-side (both when Keycloak acts as the server, and when Keycloak acts as the client, for example identity brokering) as well as all client libraries provided by Keycloak
answer_text:
We can use dual hybrid approach to maintain backward compatibility while in transition period.

Dual hybrid architecture means we will include booth legacy and quantum safe signatures.
We have to consider downgrade attack when attacker removes quantum safe signature. This has to be configured on the validator side.


Apache Santuario supports use of custom keys for signing and encryption. We need to implement key registration while initializing Santuario in `XMLSignatureUtil` and `XMLEncryptionUtil`  classes.
thread_text:
ISSUE #48825: Investigate and plan what is needed for SAML 2.0 to be PQC ready
Author: stianst
Date: 2026-05-08T08:33:23Z
Labels: priority/blocker, kind/task, team/core-protocols
State: closed

[c0]
### Description

Many of the algorithms used by SAML 2.0 endpoints and assertions are not considered PQC-safe. We need to investigate what new algorithms we need to support, including reviewing if some hybrid signing algorithms are required. This should cover all usage of cryptography in Keycloak in SAML 2.0 endpoints and assertions, including server-side (both when Keycloak acts as the server, and when Keycloak acts as the client, for example identity brokering) as well as all client libraries provided by Keycloak

It should go without saying that the approach should be based on standards and specifications; this is vital for interoperability as well as from a security perspective.

As part of the investigation provide links to a document containing notes from the investigation, including findings and required actions.

The outcome of this investigation should be a refined issue added to https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/43690, including adding sub-issues as applicable.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @stianst 2026-05-08T08:33:59Z:
Some notes from previous discussions:
* SAML for clients and identity brokering  
  * There is an initiative to add new PQC algorithms for XML/SAML (see this [W3C issue](https://github.com/w3c/strategy/issues/484)). The new RFC is in progress in [rfc9231bis](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-eastlake-rfc9231bis-xmlsec-uris-06). It seems that the idea is adding this new four PQC algorithms (three for signatures and one for key derivation/encryption):  
    * HSS/LMS: Hierarchical Signature System / Leighton-Micali Signatures (Supported in JDK 21 and BC 1.79)  
    * ML-DSA: Module Lattice \- Digital Signature Alorgithm (Supported in JDK 24 and BC 1.79)  
    * SLH-DSA: Stateless Hash-based \- Digital Signature Alorgithm (BC 1.79)  
    * ML-KEM: Module-Lattice Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism (Supported in JDK 24 and BC 1.79)  
* There is also a paper from the past year [Post-quantum XML and SAML Single Sign-On](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/828) that used java, BC, apache santuario and opensaml to implement a PoC about SAML/XML/PQC integration. The paper forked santuario and added some of the algorithms (previous names, this is a mess). Reading it very quickly I think that only signatures are implemented. This is the [repo](https://github.com/PQSAML/index) that links to other repos.  
* So, there are gaps and missing points (not even the names for the algorithms are defined in rfc9231bis now). But probably the general idea is clear:  
    * The rfc9231 is going to add the new algorithms for XML signature and encryption. There are some missing parts like how to define the *\<KeyInfo\>* element for the new keys.  
    * We need to expand (contribute to) apache santuario/xmlsec to support one signature and one derivation for PQC (for example ML-DSA and ML-KEM).  
    * Integrate the new algorithms in Keycloak to be selected.
---
[c2] @pskopek 2026-06-16T11:40:04Z:
### Hybrid approach

We can use dual hybrid approach to maintain backward compatibility while in transition period.

Dual hybrid architecture means we will include booth legacy and quantum safe signatures.
We have to consider downgrade attack when attacker removes quantum safe signature. This has to be configured on the validator side.

### Santuario support for signing an ecryption quantum safe algorithms

Nobody seems to be working on support of quantum safe algorithms (e.g. ML-DSA and ML-KEM) in Apache Santuario.

Apache Santuario supports use of custom keys for signing and encryption. We need to implement key registration while initializing Santuario in `XMLSignatureUtil` and `XMLEncryptionUtil`  classes.

* There is also a paper from the past year [Post-quantum XML and SAML Single Sign-On](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/828) that used java, BC, apache santuario and opensaml to implement a PoC about SAML/XML/PQC integration. The paper forked santuario and added some of the algorithms (previous names, this is a mess). Reading it very quickly I think that only signatures are implemented. This is the [repo](https://github.com/PQSAML/index) that links to other repos.  
* So, there are gaps and missing points (not even the names for the algorithms are defined in rfc9231bis now). But probably the general idea is clear:  
    * The rfc9231 is going to add the new algorithms for XML signature and encryption. There are some missing parts like how to define the *\<KeyInfo\>* element for the new keys.  
    * We need to expand (contribute to) apache santuario/xmlsec to support one signature and one derivation for PQC (for example ML-DSA and ML-KEM).  
    * Integrate the new algorithms in Keycloak to be selected.

comments.author: pskopek
comments.body:
### Hybrid approach

We can use dual hybrid approach to maintain backward compatibility while in transition period.

Dual hybrid architecture means we will include booth legacy and quantum safe signatures.
We have to consider downgrade attack when attacker removes quantum safe signature. This has to be configured on the validator side.

### Santuario support for signing an ecryption quantum safe algorithms

Nobody seems to be working on support of quantum safe algorithms (e.g. ML-DSA and ML-KEM) in Apache Santuario.

Apache Santuario supports use of custom keys for signing and encryption. We need to implement key registration while initializing Santuario in `XMLSignatureUtil` and `XMLEncryptionUtil`  classes.

title: CVE-2026-42581 Netty HTTP/1.0 TE+CL Coexistence Bypasses Smuggling Sanitization
need_summary: Whether the Netty HTTP/1.0 TE+CL smuggling CVE-2026-42581 meaningfully affects Keycloak and how severe it is, with the answer anchored in GHSA-xxqh-mfjm-7mv9 and the maintainer’s explanation in comment c11.
security_topic: applicability of CVE severity to Keycloak's non-proxy usage
question_text: Are the Keycloak maintainers able to provide a CVSS re-score based on the Keycloak usage?
answer_text:
The short answer is: the real-world risk here is significantly lower than the NVD 9.8 suggests.

The core issue in this CVE is about HTTP request smuggling when Netty acts as a proxy, forwarding requests between a client and a backend. Keycloak doesn't do that. It's an end-application server, not a proxy. On top of that, all of Keycloak's backchannel HTTP calls (SAML artifact resolution, OAuth2/OIDC token exchange, etc.) go through Apache HttpClient, not Netty, so those paths aren't affected either.

The one scenario where this could matter is if Keycloak sits behind a reverse proxy that happens to accept HTTP/1.0, reuses backend connections, and handles the Transfer-Encoding/Content-Length conflict differently than Netty does. In practice, most modern proxies like nginx, HAProxy, or Envoy either reject HTTP/1.0 with chunked encoding or normalize the headers before forwarding, so this is a pretty narrow window.

With that in mind, my personal take is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N 5.4 Medium. The 9.8 on NVD is accurate for Netty used in proxy mode, but that's not how Keycloak uses it.

title: Management endpoint doesn't pick up HTTPS truststore
need_summary: Whether the management HTTPS interface should inherit the main HTTPS mTLS truststore settings or default to the system truststore, which the maintainers note would weaken expected security, with the anchor being the linked management-interface and mutual-TLS docs plus the stated `--https-management-client-auth=none`/inheritance behavior.
security_topic: inheritance of mTLS truststore settings for management HTTPS endpoint
question_text:
When [configuring trusted certificates for mTLS](https://www.keycloak.org/server/mutual-tls), setting:
```
--https-client-auth=required
--https-trust-store-file=/path/to/file
```
also enables the client auth for the management endoint
```
--https-management-client-auth=required
```
but the truststore file setting doesn't seem to be picked up.
answer_text:
In the [guide](https://www.keycloak.org/server/management-interface#_tls_support), we explicitly say:
> When these options are not explicitly set, the TLS parameters are inherited from the default HTTP server.

So I agree the mTLS settings incl. the truststore should be inherited from the main HTTPS interface.

ISSUE #48593: Management endpoint doesn't pick up HTTPS truststore
Author: tkyjovsk
Date: 2026-04-29T15:00:38Z
Labels: kind/bug, priority/important, area/dist/quarkus, team/cloud-native, release/26.7.0
